source.title: Probing the Robustness of Large Language Models Safety to Latent Perturbations
source.authors: Tian-Le Gu; Kexin Huang; Zongqi Wang; Yi-Xu Wang; Jie Li; Yuanqi Yao; Yang Yao; Yu-Jiu Yang; Yan Teng; Ying-Chun Wang

page_placements.theme: Steering for unrelated purposes and generic activation perturbations erode refusal

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper evaluates random and gradient-based latent activation perturbations, not a harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means refusal direction or its ablation/addition. Its results therefore do not test any listed version of the claim. It cites the original source in its references but does not test its method.
record.gate_note: The paper reports safety effects of latent activation attacks and adversarial training against those attacks. These use random or harmful-suffix-gradient perturbations, not the claimed single refusal direction, so the results are recorded as findings about a related but different mechanism (versions ["none"]).
record.test_reason: The study injects normalized Gaussian random vectors (ASArandom) or sign-gradients of a harmful target-suffix loss (ASAgrad) into hidden states. It also trains against such perturbations (LAPT). It never computes a harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means direction, never ablates or adds one, and never edits weights to remove one. Arditi et al. appears only in a list of activation-steering works in Related Work. Its results concern a related but different mechanism: generic latent-perturbation fragility.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that current alignment is shallow, so small latent perturbations re-trigger unsafe outputs. They report that LAPT improves robustness to such perturbations while preserving general capabilities.
record.recipe_differences: The study injects normalized random vectors or gradients from harmful target suffixes at selected layers and generation steps. It does not derive or ablate a harmful-minus-harmless mean-activation refusal direction, nor add that direction.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported outcome varies with perturbation type (random versus gradient-based), layer, generation length, and random seed. The paper reports seed variation for MASR and PASR and says attack success grows with generation length.

fits_no_version.finding: Mean/std-normalized random Gaussian perturbations at single intermediate layers yield harmful compliance on most AdvBench prompts (MASR 0.89–0.99) in base and instruct models. Harmful-suffix gradient perturbations usually raise PASR further.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Safety-aligned LLMs lack local robustness to random or gradient-based activation perturbations unrelated to a specific refusal direction.

fits_no_version.finding: Applying ASA before GCG raises MASR over GCG alone in six models, e.g. Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct 0.14 to 0.93.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Latent perturbation attacks compose with prompt-based jailbreaks.

fits_no_version.finding: Layer-wise adversarial patch training with interpolation lowers ASA success on the ASABench test split. General-task accuracy stays within about 0.05.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Latent adversarial training against random perturbations improves robustness to latent attacks.

record.problems: The core attack evaluation uses the first 100 AdvBench samples. Safety judgments rely on QwQ-32B, whose reported accuracy against human labels is 0.79. Main attack results generally lack uncertainty estimates; seed variability is reported only for two models. The study does not directly test the claimed direction.
record.rows_left_out: Did not extract figure-only ASA ASR values from Figures 2 and 9 because the flattened chart text does not securely map every displayed value to a model and metric. Also omitted LAPT general-capability scores and additional safety-benchmark results because they concern the study's separate training intervention rather than a listed claim version.

untested.parts: No difference-in-means direction is extracted, ablated or added; there is no capability check of such an intervention.
No weight-orthogonalization or abliteration is tested.
No test of whether jailbreaks (GCG, or the study's ASA) suppress the refusal direction. LAPT trains against random perturbations, not against the direction's ablation.
No comparison of single vs multi-dimensional refusal representations.
Harmfulness and refusal representations are not separated.
No transfer of a direction across languages, variants or base/instruct stages. Base and instruct models are only attacked separately.
No test of how training determines the existence of a refusal direction.
Reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1-Distill, Fig. 9) are only attacked with random perturbations; the refusal direction is not examined.

record.verdict_notes: Results the rows omit do not bear on any version: Table 2 (refusal-suffix vs harmful-suffix gradients), Fig. 9 (reasoning models), Table 6 (seed variation), Table 7 (LAPT on AdvBench and HEx-PHI). The judge is QwQ-32B, with 0.79 accuracy against human labels. Main results use 100 AdvBench prompts.

versions.untested_parts: No difference-in-means direction is found, ablated, or added; no test of whether such an intervention removes or induces refusal or preserves capabilities.
No weight edit that removes the claimed direction is evaluated.
The attacks perturb activations randomly or along a harmful-suffix loss gradient; the study does not test suppression of the claimed direction or training against its ablation.
No comparison of one direction with an affine subspace, cone, or additional refusal directions.
No separation of harmfulness judgment from refusal decision is tested.
No transfer test of the claimed direction across languages, model variants, or base/instruct stages.
No test of how refusal-training choices determine whether the claimed direction exists.
Reasoning models are tested for susceptibility to activation steering, not for the claimed refusal direction or its causal role.

source_check.notes: The paper's numbers disagree with each other. Table 1 ASArandom for Llama-3.1-8B (Base 0.99/0.69, Instruct 0.96/0.41) differs from Table 6 at seed 42, the stated main-text seed (0.98/0.66, 0.92/0.42), and Fig. 10 shows other PASRs again. LAPT keeps capabilities only by interpolating with the original model so CommonsenseQA stays within 0.05 of baseline.

statements.correction: Table 1 ASArandom MASR: Qwen-2.5-7B Base 0.96, Instruct 0.89; Llama-3.1-8B Base 0.99, Instruct 0.96. MASR = share of 100 AdvBench prompts where at least one layer's injection succeeds (QwQ-32B judge). Best single layer PASR = 0.55, 0.45, 0.69, 0.41. Fig. 2 covers 8 models and Llama-2-13B-Chat has the lowest MASR. Table 6 (seed 42) gives Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct MASR 0.92. Table 4: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct GCG 0.14 -> GCG+ASA 0.93 (ASA applied before GCG, 20 tokens generated, GCG 100 steps).
statements.problem: The numbers are right, but the 0.89-0.99 MASR range covers only the four Table 1 models, and the statement presents it as general to base and instruct models. MASR counts a prompt as a success if injection at any one of all intermediate layers works, with each layer tried separately. Read as one layer being enough, it overstates: the best single layer (PASR) gets 0.41-0.69. The GCG figures are right.
